cards.front: How is relatedness between cells read in the small-subunit ribosomal RNA approach, and what does a smaller difference usually mean?
cards.back: From differences in a molecule every cell shares, not from how cells look. Fewer differences usually mean a more recent common ancestor.
cards.why: Small changes pile up in small-subunit ribosomal RNA as lineages separate.
cards.quote: Relatedness is read from differences in a molecule every cell shares, not from how a cell looks

cards.front: Why do ribosomal RNA difference scores only rank closeness roughly, rather than dating splits?
cards.back: Changes pile up faster in some lineages than others, and over the deepest splits repeated changes at one site blur the count. The scores neither date splits nor identify an ancestor.
cards.quote: So the scores rank closeness roughly; they do not date splits or identify an ancestor

cards.front: Name the four things every cell has.
cards.back: A plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA as its genetic material, and ribosomes.
cards.quote: Every cell has a plasma membrane (the lipid boundary of the cell), cytoplasm (the contents inside the membrane, outside any nucleus), DNA as its genetic material
cards.section: Three domains from one molecule

cards.front: A eukaryote is a cell, or an organism made of cells, with a {{c1::nucleus}}: a membrane-enclosed compartment holding the DNA.
cards.back: Bacteria and archaea have no nucleus.
cards.quote: A eukaryote is a cell, or an organism made of cells, with a nucleus: a membrane-enclosed compartment holding the DNA.
cards.section: Three domains from one molecule

cards.front: What are the three domains of life?
cards.back: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
cards.quote: The three domains proposed in 1990 by Woese, Otto Kandler and Mark Wheelis, Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, are still the standard labels
cards.section: Three domains from one molecule

cards.front: Where do many-gene trees place the eukaryotes relative to the archaea?
cards.back: Nested inside the archaea, closest to the Asgard archaea. Whether eukaryotes branch within or beside the Asgard group is still debated.
cards.quote: many-gene trees nest eukaryotes inside the archaea, closest to the Asgard archaea
cards.section: Three domains from one molecule

cards.front: What combination of membrane-lipid features marks archaea, and what do bacteria and eukaryotes mostly use instead?
cards.back: Archaea: isoprenoid chains, ether bonds, and a glycerol that is the mirror image of the bacterial one. Bacteria and eukaryotes mostly use fatty acids joined by ester bonds.
cards.quote: The archaeal mark is the combination: isoprenoid chains, ether bonds, and a glycerol that is the mirror image of the bacterial one
cards.section: Three domains from one molecule

cards.front: A newly cultured microbe has ether bonds in its membrane lipids. Does that alone show it is an archaeon?
cards.back: No. Some bacteria and some eukaryotic lipids also carry ether bonds.
cards.why: The archaeal mark is the combination of isoprenoid chains, ether bonds and mirror-image glycerol, checked against the ribosomal RNA comparison.
cards.quote: Ether bonds alone do not mark archaea, since some bacteria and some eukaryotic lipids carry them too.
cards.section: Three domains from one molecule

cards.front: Archaeal walls lack {{c1::peptidoglycan}}, the mesh of sugars and short peptides that forms most bacterial walls.
cards.back: Some methanogens have pseudomurein instead; many archaea have only a protein surface layer.
cards.quote: Archaeal walls also lack peptidoglycan, the mesh of sugars and short peptides that forms most bacterial walls.
cards.section: Three domains from one molecule

cards.front: Name the three common bacterial shapes.
cards.back: Cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods) and spirilli (spirals).
cards.quote: Bacteria come in three common shapes: cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods) and spirilli (spirals).
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: List the four steps of the Gram stain in order.
cards.back: Crystal violet, then iodine, then an alcohol wash, then a red safranin counterstain.
cards.quote: a smear is stained with crystal violet, treated with iodine, washed with alcohol and counterstained with red safranin
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: Why do Gram-positive cells such as Staphylococcus aureus stay purple after a Gram stain?
cards.back: Their thick peptidoglycan wall keeps the crystal violet-iodine complex through the alcohol wash.
cards.quote: have a thick peptidoglycan wall that keeps the crystal violet-iodine complex through the wash, so they stay purple
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: A technician Gram-stains E. coli but forgets the alcohol wash. What colour would the cells most likely appear, and why?
cards.back: Purple. The wash is the step that removes the violet from the thin Gram-negative wall; without it the violet stays in the cells.
cards.why: In Gram-negative cells the wash removes the violet, and only then does safranin turn them pink.
cards.quote: Gram-negative cells, such as E. coli, have a thin peptidoglycan wall beneath an outer membrane; the wash removes the violet and the safranin turns them pink.
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: A newly isolated cell without a nucleus stains purple in a Gram stain. Does that show it is a bacterium?
cards.back: No. Some archaea, such as methanogens with intact pseudomurein walls, also stain purple.
cards.why: The stain reads features of the envelope, not the domain.
cards.quote: The stain reads features of the envelope, not the domain, and a purple or pink cell can belong to either.
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: What is binary fission, and what is the doubling time?
cards.back: The cell copies its DNA, grows and divides into two. The doubling (generation) time is how long one round takes.
cards.quote: Bacteria and archaea usually reproduce by binary fission: the cell copies its DNA, grows, and divides into two.
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: Name the three routes of horizontal gene transfer in bacteria and what moves the DNA in each.
cards.back: Transformation: uptake of DNA from the surroundings. Conjugation: transfer between two cells in contact. Transduction: a bacteriophage carries bacterial DNA between cells.
cards.quote: In transduction a bacteriophage, a virus that infects bacteria, carries bacterial DNA from one cell to another.
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: A recipient bacterium gains a gene only when it touches living donor cells. Free donor DNA added to the medium does nothing, and no phage is present. Which route of gene transfer is acting?
cards.back: Conjugation.
cards.why: Conjugation needs two cells in contact; transformation would work from free DNA, and transduction needs a phage.
cards.quote: In conjugation DNA passes between two cells in contact.
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: A culture of E. coli in rich medium at 37 degrees C doubles every 20 minutes. Starting from 50 cells, with exponential growth, how many cells are there after 2 hours?
cards.back: g = 120 min / 20 min = 6 doublings. N = 50 x 2^6 = 50 x 64 = 3,200 cells.
cards.quote: N = N0 x 2^g, where g = elapsed time / doubling time
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: A bacterial culture grows exponentially from 500 cells to 4,000 cells in 90 minutes, with no lag and no deaths. What is the doubling time?
cards.back: 4,000 / 500 = 8-fold = 2^3, so 3 doublings. 90 min / 3 = 30 minutes per doubling.
cards.why: Divide the time by the number of doublings, not by the fold change.
cards.quote: g counts generations; 2^g is how many-fold the population has grown
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: The Asgard archaeon MK-D1 doubles roughly every 20 days. How long would a culture take to grow 64-fold, first with no lag and then with a 30 to 60 day lag phase?
cards.back: 64 = 2^6, so 6 doublings x 20 days = 120 days. With the lag, about 150 to 180 days.
cards.why: Growth is set by the number of generations, not by the hours.
cards.quote: Growth is set by the number of generations, not by the hours.
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: A bacterial culture in a closed flask is counted for a day. Early counts fit N = N0 x 2^g, but later counts fall far below the prediction. Why?
cards.back: The exponential model assumes every cell divides once per doubling time, none die, and food and space never run short. It fails once food runs short or cells die.
cards.quote: The model fails once food runs short or cells die.
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: Why does a short generation time give a bacterial population more opportunity to change?
cards.back: Each generation is another chance for a mutation or a transferred gene to be copied, so more generations per unit time mean more chances.
cards.quote: each generation is another chance for a mutation or a transferred gene to be copied
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping

cards.front: Why is protist an informal name rather than a natural group?
cards.back: It covers any eukaryote that is not an animal, plant or fungus, and those organisms belong to many separate branches of the eukaryote tree.
cards.quote: protists belong to many separate branches of the eukaryote tree, and their classification keeps changing
cards.section: Protists: a word for "everything else"

cards.front: Euglena is kept in dim light in a medium rich in organic food. How can it still get energy and carbon?
cards.back: By absorbing organic food. Euglena is mixotrophic: it photosynthesizes in light and absorbs organic food when light is poor.
cards.quote: and is mixotrophic: it can photosynthesize in light and absorb organic food when light is poor
cards.section: Protists: a word for "everything else"

cards.front: The gut protist Monocercomonoides has no detectable mitochondrion. What does its genome suggest about this?
cards.back: The organelle was lost in that lineage, not never present. Mitochondria are not universal among eukaryotes, and lacking something does not make a lineage primitive.
cards.quote: its genome suggests the organelle was lost in that lineage, not that it never had one
cards.section: Protists: a word for "everything else"

cards.front: Fungi were long grouped with plants. Where do their sequences place them, and what does that show?
cards.back: Closer to animals. The shared molecule, not the look, places an organism.
cards.quote: They were long grouped with plants, but their sequences put them closer to animals
cards.section: Protists: a word for "everything else"

cards.front: What are hyphae, and what tough polymer do fungal walls contain?
cards.back: Thin threads that together form a mycelium. The walls contain chitin, also found in insect exoskeletons (and glucans).
cards.quote: fungal walls hold glucans as well as chitin
cards.section: Fungi digest outside the body and partner with roots and algae

cards.front: How does single-celled yeast reproduce, and what species is baker's yeast?
cards.back: By budding. Baker's yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
cards.quote: baker's yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae
cards.section: Fungi digest outside the body and partner with roots and algae

cards.front: Give the order of steps in the schematic fungal sexual cycle.
cards.back: Plasmogamy, then a dikaryon (two separate haploid nuclei), then karyogamy into one diploid nucleus, then meiosis to haploid spores.
cards.quote: from plasmogamy through the dikaryon and karyogamy to meiosis
cards.section: Fungi digest outside the body and partner with roots and algae

cards.front: A fungal cell in a sexual cycle contains a single diploid nucleus. Which steps have happened, and what comes next?
cards.back: Plasmogamy and karyogamy have both happened. Next is meiosis, giving haploid spores.
cards.why: The dikaryon has two separate haploid nuclei; karyogamy fuses them into one diploid nucleus.
cards.quote: from plasmogamy through the dikaryon and karyogamy to meiosis
cards.section: Fungi digest outside the body and partner with roots and algae

cards.front: In arbuscular mycorrhizae, where does the fungus grow in the root, and do plant and fungus share cytoplasm?
cards.back: Into cells of the root cortex, inside the cell wall but outside the cell membrane, forming arbuscules. The plant membrane folds around each, so they never share cytoplasm.
cards.quote: inside the cell wall but outside the cell membrane, and forms branched exchange structures called arbuscules
cards.section: Fungi digest outside the body and partner with roots and algae

cards.front: What do plant and fungus trade in a mycorrhiza?
cards.back: Carbon from the plant for mineral nutrients, especially phosphorus, from the fungus.
cards.why: The mycelium extends far into the soil, beyond the roots.
cards.quote: plant and fungus trade carbon from the plant for mineral nutrients, especially phosphorus, from the fungus
cards.section: Fungi digest outside the body and partner with roots and algae

cards.front: Phosphate fertilizer is added to a soil whose chemistry locks most of it away, so the phosphorus a crop can take up barely changes. Predict the effect on the crop's gain from its mycorrhizal fungus.
cards.back: Little change expected. The benefit usually falls only when the fertilizer raises the phosphorus the plant can actually take up; if soil chemistry locks it away, uptake barely changes, so the fungus's phosphorus benefit is not expected to fall.
cards.why: The lesson says the benefit usually falls if the fertilizer raises the phosphorus the plant can actually take up, and that soil chemistry can lock phosphate away.
cards.quote: Usually less, if the fertilizer raises the phosphorus the plant can actually take up (soil chemistry can lock phosphate away).
cards.section: Fungi digest outside the body and partner with roots and algae

cards.front: What partners make up a lichen?
cards.back: A fungus with a photosynthetic alga or cyanobacterium.
cards.quote: Lichens pair a fungus with a photosynthetic alga or cyanobacterium.
cards.section: Fungi digest outside the body and partner with roots and algae

cards.front: What is a virus made of?
cards.back: A genome, either DNA or RNA, usually enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid. T2 phage has DNA; influenza viruses have RNA.
cards.quote: A virus is a genome, either DNA or RNA, usually enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid.
cards.section: Viruses as the contrast case

cards.front: On the cellular definition of an organism, why is a virus not an organism?
cards.back: An organism is a living individual made of one or more cells. A virus has no cell structure and no ribosomes, and is copied only inside a host cell.
cards.why: This is a choice of definition, not a final verdict on what counts as life.
cards.quote: This course defines an organism as a living individual made of one or more cells.
cards.section: Viruses as the contrast case

cards.front: Why can a virus not be placed on a tree built from small-subunit ribosomal RNA?
cards.back: It has no ribosomes, so it has no small-subunit ribosomal RNA to compare.
cards.quote: A virus has no ribosomes, so it has no small-subunit ribosomal RNA to compare
cards.section: Viruses as the contrast case

cards.front: A small microbe with no nucleus is cultured from a cow's rumen. Design the tests that decide whether it is a bacterium or an archaeon, and rank them.
cards.back: Main test: score its small-subunit ribosomal RNA against known bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes. Then check lipids for the archaeal combination and the wall for absent peptidoglycan; these should agree with the RNA.
cards.why: Appearance and staining do not report the domain.
cards.quote: The RNA comparison is the main test, and lipids and wall should agree with it.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Invented data: microbe X scores 0.40 against a known archaeon, 0.11 against E. coli and 0.10 against yeast cytoplasmic ribosomal RNA (0 = no shared sequence, 1 = identical). X stains pink in a Gram stain. Classify X and justify.
cards.back: An archaeon. It groups with the archaeon and scores about equally low against bacteria and yeast. The pink stain does not count against this.
cards.why: Ribosomal RNA is the main test; the Gram stain reads the envelope, not the domain.
cards.quote: Looking or staining like a bacterium tells you nothing about the answer.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: To test whether a root system and its mycorrhizal fungi reward each other, how would you track carbon to the fungi and phosphorus to the plant?
cards.back: Feed the leaves carbon dioxide with a carbon isotope and measure label in each fungus. Give each fungus separately labelled phosphorus in a compartment only its hyphae can reach, and measure label in the plant.
cards.quote: placed in a compartment its hyphae can reach but roots cannot, and measure how much reaches the plant
cards.section: Plant and fungus rewards: a contested mechanism

cards.front: In a test of whether plants reward the more generous of two fungal partners, why add a no-choice control and a run that swaps which fungal species is generous?
cards.back: The no-choice control shows whether a fungus draws more carbon wherever it grows or only when the plant can compare partners. The swap separates partner behaviour from species identity.
cards.why: Reward is supported only if the generous fungus gets more carbon in mixed plants beyond any no-choice difference.
cards.quote: A no-choice control colonizes plants with only one fungus each, which shows whether a fungus draws more carbon wherever it grows or only when the plant can compare partners.
cards.section: Plant and fungus rewards: a contested mechanism

cards.front: E. coli doubles about every 20 minutes; MK-D1 about every 20 days. How many times more generations does E. coli pass through in the same time, and what does that imply for how fast each population can change?
cards.back: 20 days = 28,800 minutes; 28,800 / 20 = 1,440 times more generations. E. coli gets 1,440 times more chances for a mutation or transferred gene to be copied.
cards.why: Change accrues per generation, so the short generation gives more opportunities to change.
cards.quote: so an MK-D1 generation lasts 28,800 / 20 = 1,440 times as long as an E. coli one
cards.section: Bacteria: shape, envelope, fission and gene swapping
